title: Kubernetes Networking Handbook: Services, DNS, Ingress & TLS
summary: A dense field guide to how traffic reaches Pods in Kubernetes — from ClusterIP virtual IPs and kube-proxy datapath internals through NodePort and LoadBalancer, cluster DNS resolution, and L7 Ingress routing with TLS termination. Covers mechanics, trade-offs, comparison tables, and the failure modes that bite people in production.

chapters.title: Why Services Exist: The Pod IP Problem
points: Every Pod gets its own routable cluster IP; the Kubernetes network model requires all Pods to reach all Pods without NAT
Pod IPs are ephemeral: a rescheduled, rolled, or crashed Pod comes back with a different IP — nothing to hardcode
Replicas scale up/down so the set of backend IPs is a moving target; clients must not track membership
A Service is a stable virtual IP + DNS name + port that fronts a changing set of Pods
Service = stable frontend, Pods = disposable backends; this is the fundamental indirection of K8s networking
Services also provide load balancing across backends, so clients get distribution for free
Definition: 'service discovery' = finding healthy backends by name, not by IP
Example failure: Deployment with 3 replicas, client caches 10.244.1.5, rolling update kills that Pod, client 100% down
Services are cluster-scoped abstractions implemented by kube-proxy on every node, not by a central proxy box
A Service is decoupled from workload type: Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, or bare Pods can back the same Service

chapters.title: Service Anatomy: Selectors, Ports, EndpointSlices
points: Minimal Service YAML: `spec.selector`, `spec.ports[].port`, `spec.ports[].targetPort`, `spec.type`
`port` = the port the Service listens on; `targetPort` = the container port traffic is forwarded to; they are independent
`targetPort` can be a named port (`targetPort: http`) resolved per-Pod via `containerPort.name` — lets heterogeneous Pods differ
The selector is a label equality match; the endpoints controller watches Pods matching it and writes their IPs
EndpointSlice objects (v1, replaced the older single Endpoints object) hold backend IP:port lists, sharded at 100 endpoints per slice by default
Why EndpointSlice replaced Endpoints: one 5000-endpoint Endpoints object rewrote and re-broadcast entirely on every Pod change — O(n) watch traffic per event
Only Pods that are Ready are placed in the ready endpoint list; not-ready Pods appear with `conditions.ready: false`
Multi-port Service: each port entry must be named when there is more than one
`kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=my-svc` is the first debugging command when a Service returns nothing
Empty endpoints almost always means a selector/label mismatch or a failing readiness probe — not a networking bug
Services support TCP, UDP, and SCTP via `spec.ports[].protocol`; a single Service can mix them

chapters.title: ClusterIP: The Default Virtual IP
points: ClusterIP is the default type: allocates a stable virtual IP from the cluster's `--service-cluster-ip-range`
The ClusterIP is virtual and unroutable — no interface owns it, no host answers ARP for it, you cannot ping it meaningfully
Traffic to the ClusterIP is intercepted and DNAT'd on the client's own node before it ever leaves that node
Reachable only from inside the cluster (Pods, and nodes via kube-proxy rules) — never from outside
The API server allocates the IP at create time and stores it in `spec.clusterIP`; it is immutable for the Service's life
You can pin a ClusterIP explicitly with `spec.clusterIP: 10.96.0.10` if it is inside the range and free
`clusterIP: None` makes the Service headless — no VIP, DNS returns Pod IPs directly (own chapter)
ClusterIP is the substrate: NodePort and LoadBalancer are supersets that also allocate a ClusterIP
Load balancing is roughly random/round-robin per connection, not per HTTP request — long-lived HTTP/2 or gRPC connections pin to one backend
The gRPC pinning gotcha: 3 replicas, 1 client, all requests hit one Pod forever unless you use a real L7 proxy or client-side balancing
Example: `kubectl run tmp --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- curl http://my-svc.default.svc.cluster.local:80`

chapters.title: Inside kube-proxy: iptables vs IPVS vs nftables
points: kube-proxy runs as a DaemonSet on every node, watches Services + EndpointSlices, and programs the kernel datapath — it does not proxy packets itself in modern modes
iptables mode: rules in the NAT table, KUBE-SERVICES chain matches the ClusterIP:port, jumps to a KUBE-SVC-xxx chain
Backend selection in iptables mode uses the `statistic random probability` module, chained so each backend gets equal odds (1/n, then 1/(n-1), …)
The final KUBE-SEP-xxx chain does the DNAT to a Pod IP; conntrack keeps the whole connection pinned to that backend
iptables mode complexity: rule evaluation is O(n) linear list traversal, and control-plane rule sync is roughly O(n) to O(n²) at thousands of Services — measurable latency above ~5k Services
IPVS mode: uses the kernel's in-kernel L4 load balancer with hash-table lookup — O(1) datapath, far faster sync at scale
IPVS supports real scheduling algorithms: rr, lc (least connection), dh, sh, sed, nq — set with `--ipvs-scheduler`
In IPVS mode ClusterIPs are bound to a dummy interface `kube-ipvs0`, which is why they appear in `ip addr` there but not in iptables mode
nftables mode (beta/GA in recent releases) is the successor to iptables mode: same model, set-based O(1) matching, better sync performance
Debug commands: `iptables-save -t nat | grep my-svc`, `ipvsadm -Ln`, `nft list table ip kube-proxy`
Some CNIs (Cilium in kube-proxy-replacement mode) bypass kube-proxy entirely using eBPF at the socket layer — DNAT happens before the packet exists
conntrack table exhaustion is a real failure mode: `nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet` in dmesg under high churn

chapters.title: NodePort: Punching a Port on Every Node
points: `type: NodePort` allocates a port from `--service-node-port-range` (default 30000–32767) on *every* node in the cluster
A NodePort Service is a superset: it still has a ClusterIP, and NodePort traffic is DNAT'd to the same backend set
Reachable at `<any-node-IP>:<nodePort>` from outside the cluster — even nodes running zero backing Pods will forward
Pin the port with `spec.ports[].nodePort: 30080`; omit it to let the allocator pick
The listener exists on every node, so you need a load balancer or DNS round-robin in front for real availability
SNAT gotcha: with default `externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster`, the node masquerades the source IP so the Pod sees the node IP, not the real client
`externalTrafficPolicy: Local` preserves the client source IP but only routes to Pods on the receiving node — nodes with no local Pod drop/reject the traffic
`Local` gives an unbalanced distribution: 1 Pod on node A and 3 on node B means node A's Pod gets 50% of node-level traffic
`Local` doubles as a health signal: external LBs health-check the nodePort and drop nodes with no local endpoints
Non-standard high ports mean firewalls, security groups, and corporate proxies often block them — a common 'works on my cluster' failure
Legitimate uses: bare-metal clusters, local dev (kind/minikube), and as the target of an external hardware/cloud LB
Anti-pattern: exposing dozens of production apps as NodePorts instead of one Ingress — port sprawl, no TLS, no host routing

chapters.title: LoadBalancer: Asking the Cloud for a VIP
points: `type: LoadBalancer` is another superset: ClusterIP + NodePort + a request to the cloud provider for an external LB
The cloud-controller-manager watches for the type, provisions the LB, and writes the address back into `status.loadBalancer.ingress`
A Service stuck in `EXTERNAL-IP: <pending>` means no cloud controller is running or the provisioning call failed — check CCM logs
Classic cloud LB targets the NodePort on all nodes; newer 'IP mode' / target-group-binding controllers target Pod IPs directly, skipping the second hop
Cost model: one cloud LB per Service. Twenty microservices = twenty LBs = twenty monthly bills and twenty public IPs
This cost pressure is the single biggest practical reason Ingress exists — one LB fronting many services
`spec.loadBalancerClass` selects which controller handles it, enabling multiple LB implementations in one cluster
`spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges` adds CIDR-based firewalling at the LB
`allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false` skips NodePort allocation when the LB targets Pod IPs directly
Cloud-specific behavior lives in annotations (internal LB, SSL cert ARN, backend protocol, idle timeout) — non-portable by design
On bare metal there is no cloud provider: MetalLB (L2 ARP or BGP announcement) or kube-vip fill the role
It is an L4 load balancer — no host routing, no path routing, no HTTP awareness, no header inspection

chapters.title: Headless Services and Stable Pod Identity
points: `clusterIP: None` creates a headless Service: no VIP allocated, no kube-proxy rules programmed
DNS for a headless Service returns A/AAAA records for *all* ready Pod IPs instead of a single VIP
Use case: clients that must know every backend — databases, quorum systems, gRPC client-side load balancing, Kafka, Cassandra
With a StatefulSet plus a headless governing Service, each Pod gets a stable DNS name: `<pod>-<ordinal>.<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local`
Concrete: `web-0.nginx.default.svc.cluster.local` resolves to Pod web-0 specifically, surviving reschedule
`spec.serviceName` on the StatefulSet must match the headless Service name or per-Pod DNS records are never created
`publishNotReadyAddresses: true` publishes Pods before they pass readiness — required for clusters that must discover peers to bootstrap a quorum
SRV records expose named ports: `_http._tcp.my-svc.default.svc.cluster.local` returns port + target for each endpoint
Headless without a selector + manual EndpointSlice = point cluster DNS at arbitrary external IPs
Gotcha: DNS caching in client libraries defeats headless discovery — a JVM with `networkaddress.cache.ttl=-1` caches forever
Headless does no load balancing; the client picks. That is the point, and also the responsibility.

chapters.title: Cluster DNS: CoreDNS, Names, and ndots
points: CoreDNS runs as a Deployment in kube-system and is itself fronted by a ClusterIP Service (usually 10.96.0.10) named kube-dns
Kubelet injects that DNS IP into every Pod's `/etc/resolv.conf` as the nameserver
The canonical FQDN for a Service is `<service>.<namespace>.svc.<cluster-domain>` — e.g. `payments.prod.svc.cluster.local`
Same-namespace shorthand `payments` works; cross-namespace needs at least `payments.prod`
resolv.conf contains a search list: `<ns>.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local` plus any node domains
`options ndots:5` means any name with fewer than 5 dots is tried against every search domain FIRST, before being tried as absolute
Consequence: resolving `api.github.com` (2 dots) fires 3–4 failing NXDOMAIN lookups before the correct one — a real latency and CoreDNS-load problem
Fixes: use a trailing dot (`api.github.com.`), or set `dnsConfig.options` to lower ndots per-Pod
`dnsPolicy` values: ClusterFirst (default), ClusterFirstWithHostNet (required when hostNetwork: true or you get node DNS), Default (inherit node), None (fully custom via dnsConfig)
The Corefile plugin chain: `kubernetes` plugin answers cluster names, `forward . /etc/resolv.conf` sends the rest upstream, `cache 30` caches
NodeLocal DNSCache runs a per-node caching agent to cut CoreDNS load and conntrack-related UDP DNS timeouts
Debug: `kubectl exec pod -- cat /etc/resolv.conf`, then `nslookup my-svc.default.svc.cluster.local`, then check CoreDNS logs with the `log` plugin enabled

chapters.title: ExternalName and Selectorless Services
points: `type: ExternalName` with `spec.externalName: db.example.com` makes CoreDNS return a CNAME — no proxying, no VIP, no endpoints
Use it to give an out-of-cluster dependency an in-cluster name, so app config points at `mysql.prod.svc.cluster.local` in every environment
Migration pattern: start as ExternalName pointing at the legacy host, later swap to a normal selector Service when the workload moves in-cluster — clients never change
Because it is CNAME-only, ports on an ExternalName Service are ignored; the client must use the real port
Gotcha: HTTPS to an ExternalName gets the *external* hostname's certificate, so SNI/hostname verification is against `db.example.com`, not the Service name
Gotcha: CNAME to an IP address literal is invalid DNS — ExternalName cannot point at a raw IP
Selectorless Service: omit `spec.selector` and hand-write an EndpointSlice with external IP:port entries
This gives you a real ClusterIP and real kube-proxy load balancing over external backends — unlike ExternalName
The EndpointSlice must carry `kubernetes.io/service-name: <svc>` as a label to bind to the Service
Nothing manages those endpoints — no health checking, no reconciliation; you own the lifecycle
Comparison: ExternalName = DNS alias, no data path. Selectorless = full data path, manual membership.

chapters.title: Traffic Policies, Affinity, and Topology
points: `externalTrafficPolicy`: Cluster (default, SNAT, balanced, extra hop) vs Local (source IP preserved, node-local only, possibly unbalanced)
`internalTrafficPolicy: Local` restricts *ClusterIP* traffic to Pods on the same node — useful for per-node agents like log shippers
`sessionAffinity: ClientIP` pins a client IP to one backend; `sessionAffinityConfig.clientIP.timeoutSeconds` defaults to 10800 (3h)
ClientIP affinity breaks behind NAT: thousands of users behind one corporate egress IP all pin to a single Pod
Cookie-based affinity does not exist at Service level — it is an L7 concern, handled by Ingress
Topology-aware routing (`service.kubernetes.io/topology-mode: Auto`) biases traffic to same-zone endpoints to cut cross-AZ data transfer cost
It only engages when there are enough endpoints per zone to be safe; below the heuristic threshold it falls back to cluster-wide
`trafficDistribution: PreferClose` is the newer, explicit field replacing the annotation-driven hint
Cross-zone traffic is billed in most clouds — topology hints are usually a cost optimization first, latency second
Trade-off: zone-local routing can overload one zone's replicas if replicas are not evenly spread — pair with topologySpreadConstraints
`spec.ipFamilyPolicy` (SingleStack / PreferDualStack / RequireDualStack) and `ipFamilies` control IPv4/IPv6 behavior

chapters.title: Readiness, Endpoint Churn, and Graceful Shutdown
points: Only Ready Pods receive Service traffic — readiness probe failure removes a Pod from rotation without restarting it
Liveness probe restarts a container; readiness probe only gates traffic. Confusing the two causes restart storms
The removal path is racy: Pod terminating → endpoint update → kube-proxy rule sync on every node. Requests land on the dying Pod during that window
`preStop: sleep 5-15s` before SIGTERM gives the endpoint removal time to propagate — the standard fix for rolling-update 502s
`terminationGracePeriodSeconds` must exceed preStop sleep + real drain time or the kernel SIGKILLs mid-request
Terminating endpoints are published with `serving: true, terminating: true` so proxies can drain long-lived connections instead of cutting them
conntrack keeps established TCP connections on the old backend even after rules change — DNAT is per-connection, not per-packet
UDP is worse: stale conntrack entries can blackhole UDP traffic to a deleted Pod IP until the entry expires
`startupProbe` protects slow-booting apps from liveness kills without weakening the steady-state liveness interval
Readiness that only checks 'process is up' is useless — check the dependency you actually need (DB pool, cache, warm model)
Mistake: readiness probe that calls a downstream service — one downstream blip marks every replica unready and takes the whole Service out

chapters.title: Ingress: Why L4 Isn't Enough
points: Services stop at L4: they route by IP and port, and have no idea what HTTP is
Ingress is an L7 HTTP/HTTPS router: it can dispatch on Host header, URL path, and terminate TLS
Two separate things: the Ingress *resource* (declarative rules, an API object) and the Ingress *controller* (the proxy that reads and enforces them)
Creating an Ingress with no controller installed does exactly nothing — a very common first-time confusion
Common controllers: ingress-nginx, Traefik, HAProxy, Envoy-based (Contour, Emissary), and cloud-native (AWS ALB, GKE GCLB)
The controller itself is usually exposed via one `type: LoadBalancer` Service — one cloud LB fronting all your apps
This is the core economic argument: N services behind 1 LB instead of N LBs
`ingressClassName` selects which controller owns an Ingress; an IngressClass can be marked default via annotation
Ingress backends are Services, not Pods — but many controllers bypass the ClusterIP and load balance to Pod IPs read from EndpointSlices
Bypassing the ClusterIP gives per-request L7 balancing, which fixes the gRPC/keep-alive pinning problem that plagues L4 Services
Ingress only covers HTTP/HTTPS. Raw TCP/UDP needs controller-specific extensions or a LoadBalancer Service
Ingress is effectively feature-frozen; Gateway API is the successor (covered later)

chapters.title: Ingress Rules: Hosts, Paths, and pathType
points: Rule structure: `spec.rules[].host` + `http.paths[]`, each path pointing to `backend.service.name` and `backend.service.port`
Name-based virtual hosting: `api.example.com` and `app.example.com` on one IP, distinguished by the Host header
Path-based fanout: `/api` to the api Service, `/static` to the cdn Service, `/` to the frontend, all on one host
A rule with no `host` matches any Host header — useful as a catch-all default backend
`pathType: Prefix` matches on whole path *elements*: `/foo` matches `/foo` and `/foo/bar` but NOT `/foobar`
`pathType: Exact` matches the full path only, and is case-sensitive
`pathType: ImplementationSpecific` hands matching semantics to the controller — that is where nginx regex paths live
Omitting pathType is invalid in networking.k8s.io/v1; it is a required field
Conflict resolution: longer path matches win; Exact beats Prefix at equal length; host wildcards lose to exact hosts
Wildcard hosts (`*.example.com`) match exactly one DNS label — `foo.example.com` yes, `foo.bar.example.com` no
`spec.defaultBackend` catches anything unmatched instead of returning the controller's stock 404
Rewrite gotcha: without a rewrite annotation, a request to `/api/users` arrives at the backend still as `/api/users`, not `/users`
The nginx rewrite idiom pairs `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /$2` with a capture-group path `/api(/|$)(.*)`

chapters.title: Ingress TLS: Certificates, SNI, and Termination
points: `spec.tls[]` takes a list of `hosts` plus a `secretName` — the controller loads that Secret and serves HTTPS for those hosts
The Secret must be `type: kubernetes.io/tls` with exactly two keys: `tls.crt` and `tls.key`
`tls.crt` must be the full chain — leaf certificate first, then intermediates. Leaf-only is the classic 'works in Chrome, fails in curl/Java' bug
The Secret must live in the *same namespace* as the Ingress; cross-namespace certificate reference is not allowed
SNI is what makes many certs on one IP possible: the client sends the hostname in the TLS ClientHello, before HTTP, so the controller picks the right cert
TLS termination at the Ingress means the hop from controller to Pod is plaintext HTTP inside the cluster by default
TLS passthrough forwards the encrypted stream untouched to the backend — the controller cannot route on path, only SNI host
Re-encryption (backend protocol HTTPS) terminates at the edge, then opens a new TLS connection to the Pod — needed for mTLS-strict or compliance setups
cert-manager automates issuance: a ClusterIssuer plus `cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer` annotation makes the Secret appear and auto-renew
ACME HTTP-01 solves by serving a token at `/.well-known/acme-challenge/` — needs public inbound reachability; DNS-01 does not, and is the only way to get wildcard certs
Force HTTPS with `ssl-redirect` (301 on the HTTP listener) and HSTS headers; do not rely on the app to redirect
Common errors decoded: NET::ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID = host not in the cert SANs; 'default fake certificate' served = secretName wrong, missing, or in the wrong namespace

chapters.title: Annotations, Controller Features, and Gateway API
points: The Ingress spec is deliberately minimal, so every real feature landed in vendor annotations — timeouts, rate limits, auth, CORS, buffer sizes, canary weights
Consequence: an Ingress manifest is not portable. Moving ingress-nginx to Traefik means rewriting every annotation
Useful ingress-nginx annotations: `proxy-body-size`, `proxy-read-timeout`, `backend-protocol: GRPC|HTTPS`, `canary` + `canary-weight`, `auth-url` for external auth
Annotation values are strings and silently ignored when misspelled — no validation, no error, just missing behavior
Gateway API is the successor: role-oriented, typed, and portable, using CRDs instead of annotation soup
Gateway API resource split: GatewayClass (infrastructure kind) → Gateway (a listener + its TLS config) → HTTPRoute/GRPCRoute/TCPRoute (the routing rules)
Role separation is the point: platform team owns GatewayClass and Gateway, app teams own Routes in their own namespaces
Gateway API supports cross-namespace attachment with explicit ReferenceGrant, header-based matching, traffic splitting by weight, and request mirroring — all first-class, no annotations
Traffic splitting by weight makes canary and blue/green a spec feature rather than a controller extension
Ingress remains supported and widely deployed; Gateway API is the direction for new build-outs
Service mesh overlap: a mesh adds mTLS, retries, circuit breaking, and observability at L7 for east-west traffic; Ingress is north-south
Trade-off: mesh gives you the most power for the most operational complexity — do not add one to solve a routing problem Ingress already covers

chapters.title: Comparison Table: Picking the Right Exposure
points: ClusterIP — scope: internal only | layer: L4 | cost: free | use: service-to-service inside cluster
NodePort — scope: external via node IPs | layer: L4 | cost: free but port sprawl | use: bare metal, dev, LB target
LoadBalancer — scope: external via cloud VIP | layer: L4 | cost: one LB billed per Service | use: non-HTTP protocols, single high-traffic entrypoint
Ingress — scope: external HTTP/S | layer: L7 | cost: one shared LB | use: many HTTP services, host/path routing, TLS termination
Headless — scope: internal, DNS-only | layer: none | cost: free | use: StatefulSets, peer discovery, client-side balancing
ExternalName — scope: DNS alias out of cluster | layer: none | cost: free | use: naming an external dependency
Gateway API — scope: external, multi-protocol | layer: L7 | cost: one shared LB | use: portable routing, multi-team ownership
Decision rule: internal HTTP → ClusterIP. External HTTP → Ingress. External non-HTTP (TCP/UDP, e.g. Postgres, MQTT, game server) → LoadBalancer
Decision rule: need the raw client IP → externalTrafficPolicy Local, or read X-Forwarded-For at L7
Decision rule: need per-request balancing for gRPC/HTTP2 → L7 (Ingress/mesh), never a plain ClusterIP
Layering fact: LoadBalancer contains NodePort contains ClusterIP — each type adds to the one below, it does not replace it
Ingress is not a Service type; it sits in front of Services and needs one exposed controller to work

chapters.title: Common Mistakes and Gotchas
points: Selector/label mismatch — Service exists, endpoints empty, every request fails. Always `kubectl get endpointslices` first
Confusing `port` with `targetPort`: Service listens on 80, container listens on 8080, `targetPort: 80` sends traffic nowhere
`containerPort` in the Pod spec is documentation only — it does not open a port; omitting it does not break a Service
Expecting a ClusterIP to be reachable from your laptop; it is not routable outside the cluster. Use port-forward, NodePort, or Ingress
Creating an Ingress with no controller installed and waiting for an IP that never arrives
TLS Secret in the wrong namespace, so the controller silently serves its self-signed fake certificate
Uploading a leaf-only cert without intermediates — browsers pass (they cache intermediates), curl and mobile clients fail
Missing `pathType`, or assuming Prefix `/foo` matches `/foobar` (it does not)
Forgetting rewrite-target, so the backend receives the full `/api/...` path it does not have a route for
Relying on ClusterIP round-robin for gRPC and finding all traffic on one Pod because HTTP/2 multiplexes one connection
NetworkPolicy blocking DNS: a default-deny egress policy without a rule allowing UDP/TCP 53 to kube-system breaks every name lookup in the namespace
Rolling-update 502s from missing preStop drain, misdiagnosed as an application bug
High ndots causing DNS latency and CoreDNS overload for external hostnames
Using NodePort as the production entrypoint and then discovering the corporate firewall blocks 30000–32767

chapters.title: Debugging Playbook: Tracing a Request
points: Work outside-in: DNS resolves? → Ingress matched? → Service has endpoints? → Pod is Ready? → app listening on the right port?
DNS check: `kubectl run -it --rm dbg --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- nslookup my-svc.ns.svc.cluster.local`
Endpoints check: `kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=my-svc -o wide` — empty means selector or readiness
Skip the Service to isolate it: `kubectl port-forward pod/<pod> 8080:8080` and curl the Pod directly
Then test the ClusterIP: `curl http://my-svc.ns:80` from a debug Pod. Pod works but Service does not = kube-proxy or port mapping
Confirm the app binds 0.0.0.0, not 127.0.0.1 — a loopback bind is reachable in `kubectl exec` but never from another Pod
Ingress check: `kubectl describe ingress my-ing` for the assigned address and events, then read the controller's own logs
TLS check from outside: `openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host` to inspect the served chain and SNI selection
Datapath check: `iptables-save -t nat | grep <clusterIP>` or `ipvsadm -Ln | grep -A3 <clusterIP>` on the node
NetworkPolicy check: does a deny policy exist in the namespace, and does it allow both the app port and DNS?
`kubectl describe svc` shows events, allocated ports, and endpoint count in one shot
netshoot is the standard debug image: dig, curl, tcpdump, iproute2, conntrack, ipvsadm all preinstalled

chapters.title: Summary: The Whole Path in One Page
points: Request path recap: DNS name → cluster DNS returns ClusterIP → kube-proxy DNAT to a Pod IP → CNI delivers to the Pod
External path recap: cloud LB → node NodePort or Pod IP → Ingress controller Pod → TLS terminate → host/path match → backend Service or Pod
Services solve identity and L4 balancing; DNS solves naming; Ingress solves L7 routing and TLS; the mesh solves east-west policy
The three Service types layer, not compete: LoadBalancer ⊃ NodePort ⊃ ClusterIP
kube-proxy is a rule programmer, not a proxy — the kernel moves the packets (iptables / IPVS / nftables / eBPF)
Endpoints are derived from readiness, so probe correctness is networking correctness
Every stable thing (VIP, DNS name, Ingress host) is decoupled from every ephemeral thing (Pod IP, node, replica count)
Default to ClusterIP internally and one Ingress externally; reach for LoadBalancer only for non-HTTP or when you truly need a dedicated L4 VIP
For new clusters, prefer Gateway API over annotation-driven Ingress for portability and clean team boundaries
Four commands that solve most incidents: `kubectl get endpointslices`, `kubectl describe svc`, `kubectl describe ingress`, `nslookup` from a netshoot Pod
Mental model to keep: a Service is a name and a promise; the endpoints list is who is currently keeping it
